1	\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
2	
3	Standard confusion-matrix correction can reverse causal conclusions when misclassification rates vary across subgroups.
4	We derived an exact bias identity ($R^2 \geq 0.97$) that yields a diagnostic for flagging harmful correction and prescribes per-subgroup correction when $\Delta\pi > 0.15$ and $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$, validated across 11 LLM--dataset combinations spanning eight LLMs and four NLP tasks.

2	\label{sec:limitations}
3

\begin{remark}
\label{rem:asymmetric}
Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} does not require assumption~(A2).
For arbitrary asymmetric confusion matrices where the false positive rate ($\mathrm{FPR}_s$) and false negative rate ($\mathrm{FNR}_s$) may differ,
the product form $\mathrm{bias}(z, s) = \Delta\tau \cdot [B_s]_{z,1}$ holds exactly,
where $B_s = M_{\mathrm{global}}^{-1} M_s - I$, because $B_s \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$
follows from stochasticity of $M_s$ and $M_{\mathrm{global}}$ alone.
Assumption~(A2) simplifies $[B_s]_{z,1}$ to the scalar
$\pm \delta_s / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$ but is not necessary for the product structure.
Under asymmetric errors, the scalar diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) remains effective with $\pi_s = (\mathrm{FPR}_s + \mathrm{FNR}_s)/2$: the screening criterion achieves per-subgroup AUC $= 0.96$ across 48 asymmetric configurations (FPR/FNR ratios 1:5 to 5:1) and correctly identifies all harmed subgroups across 8 semi-real LLM confusion matrices (32 subgroups; Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}); end-to-end validation with asymmetric CMs appears in Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric_endtoend}.
The criterion's validity extends beyond the symmetric case because the threshold $|\delta_s|/((1{-}2\bar{\pi})\pi_s) > 1$ is equivalent to $|B_s|/|D_s| > 1$ whenever subgroups have heterogeneous overall error rates.
\end{remark}

\medskip
Equation~\eqref{eq:hurts_condition} partitions subgroups into two regimes:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textit{High-error} ($\pi_s > \bar{\pi}$): the condition reduces to $\pi_s > 0.5$, excluded by~(A4); global correction always reduces bias.
    \item \textit{Low-error} ($\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$): the condition holds whenever $\pi_s < \bar{\pi} / (2(1 - \bar{\pi}))$, which is easily satisfied: when $\bar{\pi} = 0.15$, any subgroup with $\pi_s < 0.088$ is harmed by global correction.
\end{itemize}
The mechanism is over-correction: for subgroups with near-zero misclassification ($\pi_s \approx 0$), the naive estimator is nearly unbiased, yet global inversion calibrated for $\bar{\pi}$ creates substantial bias. Debiasing is worse than doing nothing, and can reverse bias sign across subgroups (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:debiasing_hurts}).

\begin{abstract}
Large language models increasingly replace human annotators in computational social science, yet their error rates can vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic and text-feature subgroups.
When these noisy labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, the standard remedy---estimating a single confusion matrix and applying its inverse uniformly---is widely trusted to remove bias.
We prove it can do the opposite.
We derive an exact bias identity showing that global correction introduces a subgroup-level bias proportional to the interaction of error-rate deviation and effect heterogeneity, a product structure invisible to any pooled analysis.
This identity reveals that correction reverses estimated causal effect signs in 14.9\% of configurations and amplifies bias across all eight real LLMs tested.
A diagnostic corollary flags harmful correction from error rates alone, without estimating treatment effects.
Guided by the identity, we propose EC-HTE, a per-subgroup correction via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation that reduces bias by $7.4\times$ under extreme heterogeneity, with clear operating conditions ($\Delta\pi > 0.15$, $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$, $K \leq 4$) and validated across 11 LLM--dataset combinations spanning four NLP tasks\footnote{Code and data: \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ec_hte_llm_annotation-4CC8/}.}.

1	\begin{abstract}
2	Large language models increasingly replace human annotators in computational social science, yet their error rates can vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic and text-feature subgroups.
3	When these noisy labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, the standard remedy---estimating a single confusion matrix and applying its inverse uniformly---is widely trusted to remove bias.
4	We prove it can do the opposite.
5	We derive an exact bias identity showing that global correction introduces a subgroup-level bias proportional to the interaction of error-rate deviation and effect heterogeneity, a product structure invisible to any pooled analysis.
6	This identity reveals that correction reverses estimated causal effect signs in 14.9\% of configurations and amplifies bias across all eight real LLMs tested.
7	A diagnostic corollary flags harmful correction from error rates alone, without estimating treatment effects.
8	Guided by the identity, we propose EC-HTE, a per-subgroup correction via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation that reduces bias by $7.4\times$ under extreme heterogeneity, with clear operating conditions ($\Delta\pi > 0.15$, $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$, $K \leq 4$) and validated across 11 LLM--dataset combinations spanning four NLP tasks\footnote{Code and data: \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ec_hte_llm_annotation-4CC8/}.}.
9	\end{abstract}

1	\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
2	
3	Standard confusion-matrix correction can reverse causal conclusions when misclassification rates vary across subgroups.
4	Our exact bias identity ($R^2 \geq 0.97$, 11 LLM--dataset combinations) yields a diagnostic for flagging harmful correction and prescribes per-subgroup correction when $\Delta\pi > 0.15$ and $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$.
5	The framework is task-agnostic and composes with prediction-powered inference.
6	As LLM annotation becomes standard practice, our bias identity provides a principled lens for auditing any pipeline that feeds machine-generated labels into downstream causal analysis.
7	Future directions include continuous covariates, larger $K$, and joint covariate--outcome correction.
